## 1. The traditional reading, verse by verse

**Overview:** Guzik dates this prophecy to 593 BC. Quoting the scholar Block, he says the prophecy came true when Jerusalem fell in 586 BC, which confirmed Ezekiel as a prophet. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-5/

**v. 1**
- This is the fourth acted-out sign, after the three in chapter 4. Guzik says the sword matters because people don't cut hair with swords; they fight with them. It points to the attack by Nebuchadnezzar's Babylonian army. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-5/
- Quoting Feinberg, Guzik says a priest like Ezekiel wasn't allowed to shave like this. A priest's hair marked him as set apart for God (Lev. 21:5; 19:27), so shaving it usually meant losing priestly standing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-5/
- The scales show that God's judgment is careful and exact. Guzik cites Feinberg (with Jer. 15:2) and Trapp, who says God's judgments are just "to a hair's weight." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-5/
- Henry says Ezekiel is himself the sign. This shows the prophet took Jerusalem's fate to heart and didn't want the day to come. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_005.cfm
- Henry says Jerusalem had once been the "head" but had become like overgrown hair, a burden to throw off. Ezekiel cuts off all of it, not just the extra, to show that God would finish Jerusalem completely. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_005.cfm
- The Bible Hub study page says the shaving and dividing stand for Jerusalem's coming humiliation and judgment. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/ezekiel/5.htm

**v. 2**
- Guzik says the three portions of hair acted out Jerusalem's fate. The message directly contradicted the false prophets who were promising rescue. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-5/

**vv. 3–4**
- Guzik says the few hairs tied into Ezekiel's garment stand for the small group left behind and the suffering they would still face. He quotes a writer (unnamed in my excerpt) who links them to the Jews left in the land under Gedaliah after the city fell. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-5/
- Henry also links them to the small group left under Gedaliah, who were expected to hold the land while most people went into exile. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_005.cfm

**v. 5**
- Guzik says "in the center of the nations" is true in several ways. Historically, and in God's plan of salvation, Israel stands at the center of His work. Geographically, it sits where continents and empires meet. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-5/
- Quoting Wiersbe (with Ezek. 38:12 and John 4:22), Guzik says Israel was privileged, but privilege brings responsibility. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-5/
- Guzik notes that the exiles probably thought Babylon deserved judgment more. God's point is "this is Jerusalem." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-5/
- Henry pictures Jerusalem as a candle on a candlestick. It was placed among the nations to spread God's light to them and from there to the ends of the earth. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_005.cfm

**v. 6**
- Guzik says Jerusalem was worse than the pagans because she had God's law, His sanctuary and knowledge of His will. Quoting Feinberg, he says guilt is measured by how much spiritual light a people had, so the charge holds even though some deny Israel was really worse. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-5/
- Henry, using the King James wording "changed my judgments into wickedness," says the people didn't just break God's laws. They twisted them into an excuse for wickedness. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_005.cfm
- Henry says God's statutes are the terms on which He deals with people. Those who reject the terms can't expect His favour. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_005.cfm

**v. 7**
- Henry says Israel wasn't even as faithful to the true God as the nations were to their false gods. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_005.cfm

**v. 8**
- Guzik says God judges them personally here, even though He uses the Babylonian army to do it. Quoting Block, he says "I, even I, am against you" may first have been a challenge shouted before one-on-one combat. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-5/
- The Bible Hub study page says judging "in the sight of the nations" stresses how serious the sin was. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/ezekiel/5.htm

**v. 9**
- Guzik says God had never before judged His people as severely as at the Babylonian conquest. Later judgments, such as the Roman destruction, may have matched or exceeded it, but none came earlier. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-5/
- Quoting Feinberg, Guzik says the nations would be astonished, because they had never seen a nation's god treat his own worshippers this way. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-5/

**v. 10**
- Guzik says the people left in the city would suffer extremes, including cannibalism, and God would scatter the survivors. He quotes a writer who admits history doesn't record this exact event in detail. That writer thinks it surely happened, given how desperate the siege became, and points to Lam. 4:10. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-5/

**v. 11**
- Guzik says the pagan nations didn't have God's sanctuary, but Israel had it and defiled it with idols. Because they defiled it, God would "diminish" them; that is his translation's word where the BSB has "withdraw My favor." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-5/
- Henry thinks the strong wording may also look ahead to eternal punishment. He says Jerusalem's destruction was a type, or foreshadowing, of that punishment. He holds that "My eye shall not spare" is fully true only in hell, and that people who die unrepentant will perish unpitied. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_005.cfm

**v. 12**
- Guzik matches the three outcomes to the hair in v. 2: one third dies of plague and famine, one third falls by the sword, and one third is scattered with a sword chasing them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-5/

**v. 13**
- Guzik says God's anger had been building for a long time and would soon be "spent." He quotes a writer who calls the passage strongly anthropopathic (it describes God with human emotions), pointing to God's fury and jealousy, with Prov. 6:34. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-5/
- Guzik says "they will know that I, the LORD… have spoken" means that when the judgment happened, it would prove God's warnings true. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-5/
- Henry links "cause my fury to rest" to the eternal judgment he mentions under v. 11. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_005.cfm
- The Bible Hub study page says this wrath that is finally satisfied points ahead to the cross, where it was poured out on Christ (Rom. 5:9). https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/ezekiel/5.htm

**v. 14**
- Guzik says the ruin would show the surrounding nations that God is righteous. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-5/

**v. 15**
- Guzik says God would teach the nations through Israel either way. If they kept the covenant, He would teach through blessing, as in Solomon's day. Because they broke it, He would teach through judgment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-5/
- The Bible Hub study page traces the "reproach among the nations" language back to Deut. 28 and forward to Jesus' lament over Jerusalem (Matt. 23:37–39). https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/ezekiel/5.htm

**v. 16**
- Quoting Clarke, Guzik says famine and plague are pictured as poisoned arrows that kill wherever they hit. Trapp adds that, unlike Jonathan's arrows for David, these weren't a warning but meant to wound. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-5/

**v. 17**
- My sources had nothing on this verse beyond the summary below.

**Whole chapter (applications)**
- Guzik says people who receive great privilege and then reject God face heavier judgment. He warns against relying on a relationship with God while ignoring its responsibilities. He sums up the chapter as famine, plague, sword and exile. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-5/
- The Bible Hub study page says having Scripture and God's presence doesn't protect anyone from discipline. It calls God's judgments measured, as the scales show, and aimed at restoration in the end. It links the chapter to Heb. 12:5–11. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/ezekiel/5.htm
